Subject: Dedicated capacity — overage handling & throttling clarification

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Before we move forward with the committed pool proposal, procurement has a couple of clarifying questions about how Redwood handles excess usage on Dedicated pools:

1) If we exceed committed GPU-hours or token throughput in a billing period, how is that metered and billed? Do you bill per token, per GPU-hour, or both?
2) Is there an automatic throttling or graceful degradation policy once we go above commit? Will requests be queued, slowed, or routed to a hosted fallback?
3) Any standard overage pricing tiers (e.g., flat % over committed rate, or tiered pricing after certain thresholds)?
4) For forecasting, can you provide a worked example of a month where usage is 20% above commit — what would the invoice look like?

Procurement also asked for any existing policy docs we can share. Could you send the relevant policy and a sample billing workbook?

Appreciate the quick turnaround — procurement is on a tight timeline.

Thanks,
David

David —

Thanks for the clear list. High-level answers below and I attached our current overage policy PDF for detail (redwood_overage_policy_v2.pdf). I also flagged Marissa to propose pricing/discount options tied to commit tiers.

Short answers:
- Metering: We meter both sustained compute (GPU-hours) and generated tokens for billing accuracy. The primary charge for Dedicated is committed compute (GPU-hours) — excess compute and high-volume token generation are billed as overage.
- Throttling & fallback: We do not silently drop requests. Our standard behavior is: up to a small burst buffer (configurable), we absorb requests and bill overage. If usage massively exceeds capacity and impacts overall latency SLOs, routing rules may divert new requests to the hosted pool (optional) or apply short-term rate throttles at the tenant level. These controls are contract-configurable.
- Pricing approach: Typical approach is a blended overage rate: a per-GPU-hour premium and a per-1M-token rate for heavy token workloads. We can also define step-down tiers (5%, 10%, 20% over commit) with predefined multipliers.

See the attachment for the formal policy text and examples. Marissa — can you share a sample invoice calc and recommended discount structure?

Best,
Soojin

Hi David —

Attaching an example workbook (estimated-billing-example.xlsx) with three scenarios and a simple worked example for +20% usage. Highlights below:

- Commit tiers: we price committed GPU-hours monthly. Example tiers: 2xA100 equivalent / 5xA100 / 10xA100. Higher commits get steeper discounts on the base GPU-hour rate.
- Overage pricing: standard is 1.4x the committed GPU-hour rate for the first 10% over monthly commit, then 1.6x for 10–25% over, and 2.0x beyond that, unless a negotiated burst agreement is in place. Token-based billing (for heavy generation) is applied for workloads that materially increase per-token cost (e.g., long contexts + many tokens) — see workbook tab B.
- Throttling: default: soft-burst up to 10% of commit absorbed in real time. After that, either (a) route to your hosted fallback if enabled (subject to hosted pricing), (b) apply tenant-level rate-limits to keep latency SLOs intact, or (c) allow continued consumption billed at overage multipliers. Which path we take is set in the SLA.
- Discounting: for deals at or above 10xA100 commit, we can consider a 12–18% discount on committed GPU-hour rates plus a softened overage multiplier (e.g., 1.2x first 10%). For mid-sized deals (5xA100) we typically offer 6–10% and a 1.3x first-tier overage.

Worked example (from workbook):
- Commit: 5xA100 equivalent (monthly commit = 3,600 GPU-hours)
- Actual usage: 4,320 GPU-hours (+20%)
- Billing: 3,600 GPU-hours at committed rate (after commit discount) + 360 GPU-hours at 1.4x + 360 GPU-hours at 1.6x (example split).
- Net uplift on invoice: ~+26% vs committed-only invoice in this scenario (depends on token mix).

If Cloudway wants more predictable exposure, we can add a capped overage program (monthly cap as % of commit) for an extra fee. Happy to model with your actual telemetry.

—Marissa

David/So ojin/Marissa —

Quick legal/ops note to ensure the commercial language maps cleanly to implementation:

- Define meter: "GPU-hour" (measured per instance-hour weighted by GPU capacity factors) and "billable token" (per 1,000 tokens of generation). Overage is assessed on either or both depending on which drives resource consumption beyond commit.
- SLA/pricing link: add a clause that allows Redwood to apply short-term throttles if tenant-level consumption is causing sustained ( > 15 mins ) latency degradation for other tenants — throttles should be limited, logged, and escalated.
- Cap option: if Cloudway wants a capped protection, include an explicit monthly overage cap (e.g., 15% of commit) and an additional fixed fee for that protection.

Suggested contract language snippet (for insertion into SOW):
"Overage. Customer will be billed for consumption above the monthly committed compute and token allotments. Overage will be measured in GPU-hours and billable tokens and charged at pre-agreed multipliers per tier. Redwood reserves the right to apply temporary rate-limiting if Customer consumption materially degrades platform latency; such actions will be used sparingly and preceded by reasonable notice when practical."

I'll prepare a short amendment draft if you want — can have a redline by EOD tomorrow.

Cheers,
Dev
